entry.title: Ghost Font uses motion and decoys to create text readable by humans but not by leading AI models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Ghost Font is an experimental anti-AI font that displays messages through motion in video form, making the text readable to humans but difficult for AI models like Claude Fable and GPT Sol 5.6 Ultra to decode. Unlike traditional fonts, Ghost Font uses moving dots and decoy messages to obscure the real text, preventing AI from reading it from static images or screenshots. The project builds on earlier efforts like the 2013 ZXX font, which was designed to evade OCR software but is now easily read by modern AI. Ghost Font aims to explore the limits of AI visual perception and preserve human creativity by creating shareable messages that AI cannot easily interpret. Potential applications include more secure CAPTCHAs and benchmarking AI progress in video-based text recognition.

entry.title: Apple sues OpenAI and former employees for alleged trade secret theft involving unreleased technologies [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Apple has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI and former employees, including Chang Liu and Tang Tan, accusing them of stealing trade secrets related to unreleased Apple technologies for OpenAI's benefit. The complaint alleges that Tan, a former Apple VP of product design, used confidential information during job interviews to extract more insider knowledge and directed candidates to bring Apple hardware components to OpenAI interviews. The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, claims Apple raised concerns with OpenAI in February 2026 but received no response. Apple accuses OpenAI's leadership and staff of normalizing such misconduct, which it says underpins OpenAI's emerging hardware business. OpenAI's hardware efforts are led by former Apple design chief Jony Ive, who joined OpenAI after its acquisition of his startup io Products.

entry.title: Decispher builds AI coding agent context by capturing and structuring tacit team knowledge from Slack, GitHub, and Jira to prevent context-blind code changes [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: AI coding agents can perfectly read code but often miss the tacit team knowledge behind design decisions, leading to removal of important safeguards or workarounds. Decispher addresses this gap by passively capturing contextual knowledge from Slack channels, pull requests, and ticket discussions without requiring engineers to write it down. Decispher organizes this captured information into structured types like decisions, constraints, and history, then fuses overlapping fragments into a canonical knowledge graph that reflects how senior engineers reason about code. This graph helps AI agents access relevant context on demand, reducing the risk of context-blind code changes that could break critical invariants or workflows.

entry.title: Startups face growing technical debt as they embed core backend logic in LLM prompts, leading to rising costs and operational challenges [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Startups rapidly prototyping AI products often embed critical application logic within large language model (LLM) prompts during early development, which initially appears cost-effective but becomes problematic as usage scales. This approach leads to increased costs, latency, and non-deterministic outputs, making debugging and maintenance difficult because business rules and workflows are encoded in natural language rather than traditional backend code. Founders and technical teams report that while LLMs are valuable for prototyping and handling ambiguous tasks, many workflows eventually require migration to more stable, efficient systems such as fine-tuned models or rule-based pipelines. The main challenge is identifying which parts of the workflow truly need open-ended reasoning versus deterministic processing, as many teams lack instrumentation to measure this. The resulting technical debt creates a production gap where AI systems are hard to reason about and support, highlighting the need to treat LLMs as a prototype layer rather than permanent backend infrastructure.

The approach includes designing agent contexts like filesystems and pairing them with local search to maximize efficiency within limited model context windows.

entry.title: GitHub project launches Agents-Sandbox, an educational lab for AI agent architectures using LangChain and local Ollama server [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Agents-Sandbox is an educational platform hosted on GitHub that offers a collection of runnable AI agent architectures built on LangChain and a local Ollama server. Each agent variant runs as a separate command-line interface, allowing users to study individual AI mechanisms through logs and experiment with different models and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) techniques. The platform includes various agents such as chatbots with memory, tool-calling bots, and hybrid models combining chat and document retrieval, with support for multiple RAG backends like Numpy, Chroma, LlamaIndex, and Haystack. Users can interact with agents via commands to load skills, ingest documents, and manage memory, facilitating hands-on learning and evaluation of AI agent behaviors in a modular environment.

entry.title: AI researchers debate job automation risks and recursive self-improvement at International Conference on Machine Learning in Seoul [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: At the International Conference on Machine Learning in Seoul, AI researchers discussed concerns about AI automating their jobs and the potential for recursive self-improvement, where AI could accelerate its own development without human input. Princeton professor Arvind Narayanan argued that AI lacks the creativity needed for major breakthroughs, suggesting researchers will focus more on hypothesis generation while AI handles experiments. Researchers from OpenAI and other institutions presented work on AI models improving other AI systems, with some predicting AI could match human post-training capabilities by the end of the year, though creativity remains a human advantage. OpenAI executives outlined timelines for AI reaching research intern and full researcher skill levels by 2028, highlighting the industry's race toward advanced AI research automation.

entry.title: How 'Eggmaxxing' Became the Latest Fertility Quest
entry.summary: Among the many private group chats circulating through Silicon Valley these days, one of the more unusual ones is a thread called "To Make an Omelette." The chat, which was started last year, numbers more than 80 women, including tech founders and other white-collar professionals. (It was originally assembled by Aella, a figure within the Bay Area's AI rationalist scene, who is also a pseudonymous sex worker.) I spoke with several "To Make an Omelette" participants, most of whom did not want to share their identities publicly given the sensitive topic of the group's conversation: female fertility-and how they can produce more eggs. The women, mainly in their 20s and 30s, join because they are freezing their eggs or planning for it. The procedure is a linchpin of fertility treatments such as in vitro fertilization, which now accounts for more than 2% of births in the U.S. every year. Doctors usually advise women under 35 that they should plan for one to two rounds of egg freezing to harvest 15 eggs, a number that offers good odds of having one child. "To Make an Omelette" emerged to support women who are banking-or at least attempting to bank-dozens and dozens of eggs, perhaps 100 or more. They belong to a niche but growing community of women-call them eggmaxxers.

entry.title: How to Conduct a Competitive Analysis with Google Gemini [ * ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Decisions about when, where, and how to expand a business are always fraught with uncertainty. The prospect of growing the business and reaching new customers with novel offerings is enticing, but a false step can be extremely costly. A well-researched competitive analysis can reduce this risk by surfacing potential stumbling blocks at the very beginning of the brainstorming process. Historically, these analyses have been extremely time-consuming, as they have required business leaders to manually look through hundreds of pages of annual reports, painstakingly track competitor pricing, and synthesize consumer sentiment from social media and review websites. With Gemini, organizations can quickly generate an initial competitive analysis report, helping leaders decide whether a new venture is worth pursuing. Step 1: Prompt Gemini To get the best results, you'll want to be as specific as possible. Consider using a prompt that gives Gemini a persona and a clear objective, which will help ensure that Gemini approaches the task from the viewpoint of a business leader, rather than a casual searcher. Here's an example: I am a CMO conducting a competitive analysis. My company is considering expanding into [a new line of business]. Generate a list of the top five competitors in the [industry] industry and include their pricing, strengths, weaknesses, and target audience. If you type your prompt into the "Ask Gemini" box, Gemini will return a high-level briefing in just a few seconds. If you want something more comprehensive, click on the "Tools" button and select "Deep Research," then run your prompt. Gemini will create a research plan. Review the plan, suggest any needed tweaks, and then click "Start Research." For a Deep Research report, Gemini will produce a competitive analysis with citations and sources. Step 2: Interrogate the Output Gemini's initial response or report should be treated as a starting point, not a finished analysis. While the model can quickly surface competitors, pricing models, and positioning, you still need to use your own industry and market expertise to evaluate and refine those insights. First, simply check to make sure that Gemini's output aligns with your knowledge of the space. Is the list of competitors complete, or are any key players missing? Does the pricing reflect what you've seen in the real world? Ask Gemini to fill in any gaps. You might go back and forth several times, with each response containing more complete and nuanced information. This iterative process helps ensure that Gemini delivers the exact details you need to determine how to move forward. Step 3: Create a Five-Year Plan Once you have a clearer picture of the competitive landscape, you can begin to map out a strategic direction. Here again, Gemini can get you started. Try this sample prompt: Okay, I am going to try to convince my CEO that we should expand into [line of business]. Draft a concise, competitive strategy outline for the next five years for the [industry] industry across North American markets with potential goals, strategies, and tactics. You can also add any relevant sources so Gemini has more information about your organization. Gemini's plan may include initial goals for market penetration, specific tactics to support strategic pillars, and a year-by-year execution roadmap. Just as with the competitive analysis report, you should bring your own judgment and expertise to this five-year plan. Build on what you find helpful, and push back on areas that feel weak or impractical. Keep working with Gemini until you have an outline that is both realistic and aligned with your goals. Step 4: Make the Work Your Own Before presenting your expansion plan to leadership, revise it to include essential details that aren't included in Gemini's training data: your internal capabilities, budget constraints, existing customer relationships, and leadership priorities. Replace any generic language with details grounded in your market knowledge, and adjust timelines or tactics based on what your team can realistically execute. You may also want to incorporate case studies or data points from your company's previous efforts to strengthen your case. With Gemini, you can complete the comprehensive background work needed for an expansion effort that succeeds in the real world.

entry.title: Meta Finds a New Way to Spend a Fortune on AI [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: The AI laggards are going on the offensive! Meta Platforms on Thursday unveiled its latest AI model, Muse Spark 1.1, a day after SpaceX's AI unit introduced a new model of its own. Like SpaceX, Meta claimed its new model delivers performance comparable to that of established models from AI labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. We'll have to wait a few days to see whether developers agree. (Meanwhile, OpenAI unveiled its latest models, GPT 5.6). What may be most significant, however, is Meta's apparent intention to spend a fortune subsidizing usage of its new model in hopes of pulling market share from its rivals. In an interview with Bloomberg, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Meta's pricing for what users would pay to use the models would be "very aggressive and attractive." Bloomberg's report said Meta's prices would be about a quarter of those advertised by top models from Anthropic and OpenAI-in other words, dirt cheap.
